clue.text: Finish alternative home for witch

parts.note: to finish is to end
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A witch is advised to wind up her affairs and look for another place to live.
explanation.walkthrough: The Witch of Endor is the medium Saul consults in the First Book of Samuel.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible, the village where Saul visited the medium is named for that witch, so it is literally her home.

clue.text: "The de'il's away wi' him", said Burns

definitions.text: "The de'il's away wi' him", said Burns

parts.words: "The de'il's away wi' him", said Burns
parts.note: the Robert Burns song 'The Deil's Awa wi' th'' tells of the devil dancing off with a tax officer of the Scottish excise

explanation.surface: A line of Scots verse in which the poet gleefully reports the devil carrying someone off.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Burns was himself a tax officer when he wrote the song, which makes the devil's victim a colleague.
explanation.definitionFit: The Burns song's title names the hated revenue collector as the one the devil takes away.

clue.text: Historian, statesman and author, but not really liked

indicators.note: something not really as written has been altered, so the word liked is rearranged

explanation.surface: A distinguished Victorian man of letters and politics who, despite it all, was not genuinely popular.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Charles Dilke was a Victorian Liberal politician and writer whose career collapsed in a divorce scandal, which gives the surface its edge.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Charles Dilke wrote Greater Britain, held office under Gladstone and was a noted Victorian writer and politician.

clue.text: Some of his impressions of Rome are evergreen

definitions.text: Some of his impressions of Rome are evergreen

parts.words: Some of his impressions of Rome are evergreen
parts.note: the Italian composer's tone poem The Pines of Rome depicts trees which are evergreen, and his Roman pieces remain perennially popular

explanation.surface: A remark that an artist's pictures of the Eternal City never go out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: His Roman trilogy is Fountains of Rome, Pines of Rome and Roman Festivals; the pines are the evergreens.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian composer wrote three orchestral portraits of the city, one of them devoted to its pine trees.

clue.text: Shakespearean nightmare

parts.note: in Richard III Queen Margaret calls Richard an evil spirit with this word, a frightening figure from bad dreams

explanation.definitionFit: The word means an evil spirit, used as an insult to Richard in Richard III, a fiend of the kind that haunts bad dreams.

clue.text: Durrell character in debacle at Cairo

indicators.note: in tells us the name sits inside the words debacle at

explanation.surface: A figure from a Lawrence Durrell novel caught up in some disaster in the Egyptian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The Alexandria Quartet is set in Egypt, so Cairo fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: The painter who gives her name to the last volume of Lawrence Durrell's Alexandria Quartet.

clue.text: Short amusing piece, or teatime cod, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of teatime cod might be some other arrangement

explanation.surface: A light sketch, or simply a fish served at tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TEATIMECOD into the ten letters of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A diminutive of comedy: a brief light comic play or sketch.

clue.text: Kingdom of daylight's dauphin, — -dawn-drawn Falcon.. hopkins

definitions.text: Kingdom of daylight's dauphin, — -dawn-drawn Falcon.. hopkins

parts.words: Kingdom of daylight's dauphin, — -dawn-drawn Falcon.. hopkins
parts.note: a quotation from Gerard Manley Hopkins's poem The Windhover with one word left blank for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A line of Hopkins's poem about a kestrel in flight at daybreak, with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line of The Windhover reads 'kingdom of daylight's dauphin, ___-dawn-drawn Falcon'; the blank is the word that fills it.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes the spotted, mottled light of early dawn in Hopkins's line.

clue.text: Writer Harriet is followed by bird on the water at Nice

indicators.note: in a down clue on means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: a martin is a bird of the swallow family
eau is French for water, as spoken in Nice

explanation.surface: A Victorian author is trailed by a bird skimming the sea on the French Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: Harriet Martineau was a Victorian journalist and social theorist.
explanation.definitionFit: Harriet Martineau was a prolific Victorian essayist, novelist and economist.

clue.text: His traveller was unfortunate

parts.note: the Elizabethan writer Thomas ... wrote the picaresque tale The Unfortunate Traveller

explanation.surface: A comment that someone's companion on the road had bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Nashe's 1594 novel is titled The Unfortunate Traveller, so the traveller in his book was literally unfortunate.

clue.text: Byron felt that while it stood, Rome should stand

definitions.text: Byron felt that while it stood, Rome should stand

parts.words: Byron felt that while it stood, Rome should stand
parts.note: in Childe Harold Byron renders the pilgrims' saying that while the great amphitheatre stands, Rome shall stand

explanation.surface: A poet's belief that the Eternal City will last as long as one monument does.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Flavian amphitheatre in Rome is the monument in the old prophecy Byron quotes in Childe Harold.

clue.text: Average score is made by Trojan prince

parts.note: par is the standard score for a golf hole, an average performance

explanation.surface: A Trojan royal hero is said to be produced by a merely middling result.
explanation.definitionFit: The son of Priam whose abduction of Helen began the Trojan War.

clue.text: Route taken by Fleur Adcock

parts.note: the New Zealand-born poet Fleur Adcock published a collection called The ... Route

explanation.surface: A note on which road a particular poet chose to travel.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleur Adcock's 1974 poetry collection is titled The Scenic Route, the picturesque way she took.

clue.text: Pye's stage queen

parts.note: the Poet Laureate Henry James Pye wrote a tragedy named for its royal heroine, a queen on the stage

explanation.definitionFit: Henry James Pye's tragedy takes the name of a queen, the same name later borne by William IV's consort.

clue.text: Statesman was pilgrim's weight

parts.note: a palmer is a pilgrim who brought back a palm leaf from the Holy Land, made possessive
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: A political leader is described as a weight belonging to a pilgrim.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Palmerston was a Victorian Prime Minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Palmerston was twice British Prime Minister and a long-serving Foreign Secretary.

clue.text: Some erratic protagonists of Harold Frederic

definitions.text: Some erratic protagonists of Harold Frederic

parts.words: Some erratic protagonists of Harold Frederic
parts.note: the American novelist Harold Frederic wrote a novel titled after the proverbially mad springtime animals

explanation.surface: A description of the unpredictable heroes of an American novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Harold Frederic's 1896 novel bears this title, and the creatures are proverbial for wild behaviour in spring.

clue.text: Household words for dangerous quarry

definitions.meaning: the title of a novel by Geoffrey Household, words he wrote
a solitary wild elephant driven from its herd, a hazardous animal to hunt

explanation.surface: Familiar sayings about prey that bites back.
explanation.walkthrough: Geoffrey Household's 1939 thriller is about a hunter who becomes the hunted.
explanation.definitionFit: Geoffrey Household's novel bears this title, and the phrase also names a savage lone elephant or other hunted beast.

clue.text: Fleming's was from Tartary

parts.note: Peter Fleming's 1936 travel book is titled after reports sent back from Central Asia

explanation.surface: A remark about where someone named Fleming's belongings came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Fleming's book of his journey across Central Asia is News from Tartary, so his tidings came from there.

clue.text: His fellow-traveller was an ass

parts.note: the Scottish author made a journey through the Cevennes with a donkey called Modestine

explanation.surface: A grumble that someone's companion on a trip was a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ass' reads as an insult but is literal: a donkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes about his walk with an animal companion.

clue.text: Many manage right crime writer

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, i.e. many
to handle is to manage

explanation.surface: A great many people can run a righteous author of detective fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: C for 'many' is a crossword convention from the Roman numeral 100.
explanation.definitionFit: Raymond Chandler wrote hard-boiled detective novels featuring Philip Marlowe.

clue.text: "She approaches; she is —" (Wilde)

parts.note: a line from Oscar Wilde with the final word left blank, a word meaning close at hand

explanation.surface: A quotation from Oscar Wilde with its last word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means near, completing the sense of someone drawing close.

clue.text: Premises vacated by Blackwood,

parts.note: Algernon Blackwood wrote a ghost-story collection titled after an unoccupied dwelling

explanation.surface: A building that someone called Blackwood has moved out of.
explanation.definitionFit: Algernon Blackwood's 1906 supernatural collection is titled The Empty House, an unoccupied building.

clue.text: Information on Stowe character in Switzerland

indicators.note: in a down clue on means the first piece sits above the second

parts.note: gen is slang for information
Little Eva is the child in Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin

explanation.surface: Facts about a heroine of an American novel, found somewhere in the Alps.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN for information is British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Geneva is the Swiss city on Lake Geneva, a place in that country.

clue.text: Steinbeck's little gem

parts.note: John Steinbeck's short novel takes its name from a precious jewel found by a diver, a small gem of a book

explanation.definitionFit: Steinbeck's novella is about a fisherman who finds a valuable jewel from an oyster.

clue.text: Time to hire detective

parts.note: to rent is to hire

explanation.surface: It is the moment to engage a private investigator.
explanation.walkthrough: Philip Trent is the sleuth of E. C. Bentley's Trent's Last Case.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Trent is the amateur sleuth of E. C. Bentley's classic Trent's Last Case.

clue.text: Spirit needing plenty of water

parts.note: a female elemental who lives in water, from Latin unda for wave, and also a strong drink one might dilute

explanation.surface: A strong drink that should be well diluted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' looks like liquor wanting dilution; it is a water nymph.
explanation.definitionFit: A water nymph from Paracelsus and de la Motte Fouque's tale, an elemental creature living in water.

clue.text: They gave Decianus the sack at Colchester

definitions.text: They gave Decianus the sack at Colchester

parts.words: They gave Decianus the sack at Colchester
parts.note: Boudicca's tribe sacked Colchester and drove out the Roman procurator Catus Decianus

explanation.surface: A tale of a Roman official being dismissed from his job in an English town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gave the sack' sounds like dismissal; it is the sacking of Roman Colchester in AD 60.
explanation.definitionFit: The British tribe led by Boudicca whose revolt sent the procurator Catus Decianus fleeing to Gaul.

clue.text: Shades of this writer feature in many black-and-white Westerns

definitions.text: Shades of this writer feature in many black-and-white Westerns

parts.words: Shades of this writer feature in many black-and-white Westerns
parts.note: old monochrome films are in tones between black and white, and many cowboy films were based on Zane's novels

explanation.surface: An observation that old cowboy films bear traces of one author.
explanation.definitionFit: Zane Grey wrote many Western novels filmed in the monochrome era, whose tones are this shade.

clue.text: Eliminate ages before start of epoch

indicators.note: before puts the first piece ahead of the next

parts.note: eras are ages

indicators.note: start of takes the first letter of the word epoch

explanation.surface: A command to wipe out whole ages before an epoch even begins.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to wipe out or delete, removing something entirely.

clue.text: They are the cardinal twentieth-century form, thought Brigid Brophy

definitions.text: They are the cardinal twentieth-century form, thought Brigid Brophy

parts.words: They are the cardinal twentieth-century form, thought Brigid Brophy
parts.note: the novelist Brigid Brophy argued that crime and suspense fiction was the defining genre of the twentieth century

explanation.surface: A critic's claim about the most important literary genre of the modern age.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspense novels and films are the genre Brigid Brophy praised as the characteristic form of her century.

clue.text: A creation of 17, and reported friend of Shelley

indicators.note: reported means the friend's surname is heard spoken, not written

parts.note: Edward John Trelawny was a friend of Shelley and Byron who cremated Shelley's body

explanation.surface: A fictional figure invented by one author, said to be a companion of a Romantic poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 is 17-down, Stevenson: Squire Trelawney appears in Treasure Island. The friend spells his name without the second E.
explanation.definitionFit: Squire Trelawney, who finances the voyage in Treasure Island, was invented by Robert Louis Stevenson.

clue.text: Be a dampener, say, to act like Richard I

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be heard rather than read

parts.note: to rain is to wet things, to be a dampener

explanation.surface: A suggestion that being a wet blanket is how to behave like the Lionheart.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard I was King of England, so acting like him is ruling.
explanation.definitionFit: To reign is to rule as monarch, which Richard I did as King of England.
